rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder closer to what can actually be reported from the supplied facts. Its strongest line, "Airbnb wants corporate travel managers to stop chasing employees for receipts," turns the launch into a concrete T&E operations story with proof gates attached. B has sharper beat separation, but "Expense software is becoming a travel distribution channel" is the kind of clever frame that collapses if the integration is just receipt forwarding. Pretty wrapper, thin floor.
gaps_in_A: "chasing down Airbnb receipts scattered across employee expense reports" is plausible, but it is not in the update. Treat it as a reporting hypothesis until a travel manager says it.
"the exact infrastructure ... that hotel chains have used to lock in corporate travel budgets" imports industry context the update did not give. It may be true, but this set does not prove it.
"A business-trends reporter or a features desk covering the future of corporate travel policy" is softer than the other beat definitions. "Features desk" is where decent angles go to nap.

The refusal of the Concur/Ramp angle as "no_journalist_shape" is too broad. The rival-software version is bad, but a narrower expense-stack integration story could be viable if the integration has real depth.
gaps_in_B: "Expense software is becoming a travel distribution channel" overstates the facts. The update says expense integrations, not booking flow, distribution, or demand generation.
"Concur, the legacy enterprise standard, and Ramp, the challenger" may be true market context, but it is not in the supplied update. In this exercise, that is an invented support beam.

"treating the expense layer as the gateway to corporate travel demand rather than building its own closed booking pipe" is a strategy claim dressed as analysis. It needs evidence before it goes anywhere near a reporter.
"Next step: `journalist-fit-check`" is the wrong first move when no journalist list exists. Pick the angle, prove the weak claim, then build a fit-checked list.
